blocks.text: Verse 6 does not set mercy against worship itself. Its contrast challenges sacrifice and burnt offerings when they are detached from hesed—steadfast, faithful care—and from knowing God. In this chapter, knowing God is more than possessing religious information or a private spiritual feeling; it includes fidelity expressed in ethical, relational, political, and worshiping life. The verse therefore should not be used to disparage Jewish worship or to oppose mercy to embodied religious practice.

The language of revival after two days and being raised on the third day first portrays communal restoration. Later readers have connected it with resurrection and Christ, but the passage does not explicitly predict Jesus’ resurrection. The opening call to return also invites interpretation: its framing and evaluation should not simply be assumed to match the repentance speech in Hosea 14.
